title: The Lost Fabergé Eggs
subtitle: Imperial Russia · after 1917
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.
grade: Muted documentary still, late-nineteenth-century Imperial Russian goldsmith's work on an old worn wooden workbench in a dim back room, warm old-gold and sapphire-blue glints against deep blue-black shadow, melancholy and uncanny, cinematic vertical composition with one centred subject, fine film grain. Single image, not a collage, no text, no signage, no hallmarks, no people, no faces, no hands.

beats.vo: A scrap dealer bought it for its gold. It was a lost Imperial Fabergé egg, found in twenty twelve.
beats.img: A small reeded yellow-gold egg about the size of a hen's egg, standing on a gold three-legged stand with lion-paw feet, hung with tiny gold leaf festoons and set with oval blue sapphire cabochons and small diamond bows, centred and filling the middle of the frame, sitting on a worn wooden workbench among dull tarnished scrap metal (bent brass spoons, an old candlestick, a small set of scales) softly out of focus around it, lit clearly by a single warm lamp so the gold glows, bright and legible at small size, the background falling softly into shadow, no people, no hands, no lettering.

beats.vo: Of fifty made for the tsars, at least six are still missing.
beats.img: An open antique fitted presentation case lined with faded dark blue velvet, its single egg-shaped hollow completely empty, centred and filling the middle of the frame on a worn wooden bench, one thin cold beam of light falling across the empty hollow, deep shadow all around, quiet and still, no egg, no people, no hands, no lettering.

facts.claim: Fifty Imperial Easter eggs were made by the House of Fabergé for the Russian tsars (Alexander III and Nicholas II), 1885 to 1916; two more were planned for 1917 but never delivered (52 commissioned)

At least six Imperial eggs are still missing as of 2026. Counts differ by source: six (Wikipedia: 44 of 50 delivered survive; History Hit; Boing Boing 15 Jul 2026; Futura-Sciences 11 Nov 2026) or seven (New York Loan 2026, citing Fabergé; Apollo 2014: 43 of 50 accounted for). 'At least six' is true under every current count; the VO avoids a single exact number

The Third Imperial Egg was made by Fabergé in 1887 for Tsar Alexander III, an Easter gift to Empress Maria Feodorovna: a reeded gold egg on a gold lion-paw stand with sapphires and diamonds, holding a Vacheron Constantin lady's watch
The egg was confiscated after the 1917 revolution and held by the Soviet state; the last record of it in Russia was a 1922 inventory, after which it was lost ('lost after the Russian Revolution')
(caption) It sold at Parke-Bernet, New York, in 1964 for $2,450 without any mention of Fabergé

A scrap metal dealer in the American Midwest bought it at a market for about $14,000 ($13,302) intending to sell it for its scrap/gold value (to be melted down); buyers thought he had overpriced it ('bought it for its gold', 'BOUGHT AS SCRAP')

(caption) An internet search for the egg and 'Vacheron Constantin' led him to the London jeweller Wartski, which confirmed the egg's identity in 2012; it was shown in London in April 2014 and sold to a private collector

Still unsolved as of 2026: Boing Boing (15 Jul 2026) 'Six of the tsars' jeweled Fabergé eggs have never been found'; Futura-Sciences (11 Nov 2026) says the count of missing imperial eggs stands at six; New York Loan (2026) says seven remain unlocated; no recovery of a missing Imperial egg reported 2024-2026
